sections.title: The guess follows the time of the story
sections.content: You know the conditional (*me gustaría*) from A2 Unit 26, and from B1 Unit 22 that it can guess about the past: *Serían las ocho cuando llegó el tren*. This lesson gives the rule that decides between the two guessing tenses: they follow the time of what you are saying. Speaking about now, guess with the future (*Estará en casa*). Telling something in the past, guess with the conditional (*Estaría en casa*). The conditional is also how you wonder aloud about a past event: *¿Por qué nadie lo impediría?* means 'Why did nobody stop it, I wonder?'

sections.title: The same guess, now and then
rows: Serán las diez. / Serían las diez.
It is probably ten. / It was probably ten.
Tendrá treinta años. / Tendría treinta años.
He is probably thirty. / He was probably thirty.
Who can be calling? / Who can have been calling?

sections.title: A guess is not a condition
sections.content: Do not confuse this conditional with the one that needs a condition: *Iría si pudiera* 'I would go if I could'. A guess has no *if* clause and no imagined situation. It says what the speaker thinks was true at that moment. It is also different from the polite conditional (*Me gustaría...*).

items.spanish: Cuando salí de casa, serían las nueve.
items.english: When I left home it was probably about nine.

items.spanish: El vecino tendría unos sesenta años.
items.english: The neighbour was probably about sixty.
Nobody answered; they were probably all asleep.
Why did nobody stop it, I wonder?
Who can have been calling at that hour?

sections.content: The guess takes its time from the story, so it often sits next to a preterite: *Cuando llegué, serían las diez*. Do not use the conditional for a guess about now, and do not use the future in a story set in the past.
